questions.prompt: Locals are declared in the order Tag a, Tag b, Tag c in one scope. In which order do their destructors run?
options: Unspecified
Only the last one is destroyed
a, b, c
c, b, a
questions.explanation: Locals are destroyed in the reverse order of construction.

questions.prompt: Given std::unique_ptr<int> p = std::make_unique<int>(1); what does 'auto q = p;' do?
options: Compiles; q and p share ownership of the int
Compiles and silently sets p to null
Does not compile: unique_ptr is not copyable
Compiles; the int is deep-copied into q
questions.explanation: Exclusive ownership means no copy constructor; you must write std::move(p).

questions.prompt: What is the effect of 'return std::move(local);' where local is a local object of the return type?
options: It prevents copy elision and forces a move, so it is usually a pessimization
It is required to avoid a copy of the local object on return
It leaves local valid and unchanged for the caller to use afterwards
It makes the return faster than plain return local by skipping the move
questions.explanation: Plain 'return local;' allows NRVO and otherwise moves automatically.

questions.prompt: draw(frame) only reads the frame during the call; the caller keeps it afterwards. Which parameter is the clearest contract?
options: Frame*
const Frame&
std::unique_ptr<Frame>
std::shared_ptr<Frame>
questions.explanation: A const reference states a non-owning, non-null, read-only borrow.

questions.prompt: A loop at 10 Hz runs for 1 hour. In one of every 5 cycles an error path skips delete[] on a 1024-double buffer. How many bytes leak? Integer.
A std::vector<double> with 2,000,000 elements is passed by value (no elision) through 3 functions in a chain, copying each time. How many bytes are copied in total? Integer.
questions.explanation: Each copy is 16,000,000 bytes; three copies: 48,000,000. Moves would copy no element data.

questions.prompt: Buffer a(5); Buffer b(std::move(a)); Buffer d(std::move(b)); { Buffer c(2); auto p = std::make_unique<Buffer>(4); Buffer e(std::move(c)); } -- if Buffer::alive counts constructed-minus-destroyed objects, what is it after the block closes? Integer.
questions.explanation: a, b and d are alive (a and b are moved-from but still objects): 3. Inside the block c, the heap Buffer and e (each move constructs a new object) bring the total to 6; e, p and c die at the closing brace, leaving 3.

questions.prompt: A vector of a copyable type with a throwing move constructor grows by doubling (capacity 1, 2, 4, 8) while 8 elements are pushed one at a time. How many element copies happen during relocations only? Integer.
questions.explanation: Reallocations happen at push 2 (1 element), push 3 (2) and push 5 (4): 1+2+4 = 7 relocations, each a copy.

questions.prompt: A teammate's class holds a raw pointer, defines a destructor, and the program crashes with 'double free' when objects are stored in a std::vector. Explain the cause and give a minimal fix using the rule of zero and another using the rule of five.
rubric: Cause: implicit copy shares the pointer; two destructors free it.
Rule of zero: use std::vector<double> or unique_ptr<double[]> and delete nothing by hand.
Rule of five: delete copies or deep-copy them and implement noexcept moves that null the source.

rubric: Samples(Samples&& o) noexcept : p_(o.p_), n_(o.n_) { o.p_ = nullptr; o.n_ = 0; }
~Samples() { delete[] p_; } (a delete of nullptr is a no-op).

questions.prompt: A class has two raw owning members initialised in the constructor's initialiser list with new double[12] and new double[20]. The constructor body then always throws. A robot attempts to construct it at 5 Hz for 2 minutes. How many bytes leak in total? Integer.
questions.explanation: A throwing constructor never runs the object's own destructor, and the members are raw pointers, so their destruction frees nothing. Each attempt leaks (12 + 20) * 8 = 256 bytes. Attempts: 5 Hz * 120 s = 600. Total 600 * 256 = 153,600 bytes. With std::unique_ptr<double[]> members the completed members would be destroyed and nothing would leak.

questions.prompt: A Buffer defines only Buffer& operator=(Buffer o) noexcept { swap(*this, o); return *this; } and the copy constructor of Buffer throws std::bad_alloc inside the statement a = b. What is the state of a afterwards?
options: a is empty (size 0) because its storage was released first
Unspecified: only the basic guarantee holds for assignment operators
a is unchanged: the copy fails before the body runs
a holds half of b's elements, because the copy stopped midway
questions.explanation: The by-value parameter o is constructed before the function body runs. When its copy constructor throws, the body (which contains the only mutation, the noexcept swap) never executes, so a is untouched: this is the strong exception guarantee. Option 0 describes the naive delete-then-new assignment; option 3 confuses a partial copy of the temporary with the target; option 1 is true of the naive version, not of copy-and-swap.

questions.prompt: Explain why std::vector relocates with std::move_if_noexcept when it grows. Show that relocation by moves cannot give the strong exception guarantee if the k-th move may throw, state what the vector does for a copyable type with a throwing move, and what is waived for a move-only type.
rubric: Strong guarantee means a throwing push_back/emplace_back leaves the vector exactly as before.
If the k-th move throws, elements 1..k-1 have already been moved from; undoing needs k-1 more moves, which may throw too, so no guaranteed rollback exists.
Copying leaves the sources intact: on a throw the new copies are destroyed and the new block freed, so the old vector is untouched.

move_if_noexcept yields an rvalue only if the move is noexcept or the type is not copyable; a copyable type with a throwing move is therefore copied (cost O(n) copies instead of O(n) moves, hence the advice to mark moves noexcept).
For a move-only type with a throwing move there is no alternative; the strong guarantee is waived and the effects are unspecified.
